messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, December 31, 2015 at 12:57:10 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I want to run this by everyone on stan-dev before
> creating the issue and starting to work on it.
>
> 1.  New density expression with normalization and vertical bar:
>
>  cauchy<norm=true>(y | mu, sigma)

I know the vertical bar signifies conditional probability, but is the
vertical bar anything more than part of the name of the density?

In other words, the vertical bar can only appear at one position in the
argument list, correct?

This seems a bit idiosyncratic from the point of view of computer
language design. Typically, syntactic elements are introduced to
signify some particular semantic. Can I write cauchy(y, mu | sigma) or
cauchy(y, sigma | mu) or cauchy(y, mu, sigma)? If not, then I wonder
whether the vertical bar serves to clarify or complicate the language.
Does it profit authors to be required to remember where the vertical
bar goes in the argument list?

--
Joshua N. Pritikin
Department of Psychology
University of Virginia
485 McCormick Rd, Gilmer Hall Room 102
Charlottesville, VA 22904
http://people.virginia.edu/~jnp3bc

> I know the vertical bar signifies conditional probability, but is the
> vertical bar anything more than part of the name of the density?
>
> In other words, the vertical bar can only appear at one position in the
> argument list, correct?
>
> This seems a bit idiosyncratic from the point of view of computer
> language design. Typically, syntactic elements are introduced to
> signify some particular semantic. Can I write cauchy(y, mu | sigma) or
> cauchy(y, sigma | mu) or cauchy(y, mu, sigma)? If not, then I wonder
> whether the vertical bar serves to clarify or complicate the language.
> Does it profit authors to be required to remember where the vertical
> bar goes in the argument list?

We'll be using it the conventional way to separate the variate/outcome
(left of bar) from parameters (right of bar).  So you'd only get
normal(y | mu, sigma), not any other bar placement.  And in fact
for all of our current densities, there's only argument to the left.  If
we had a bivariate distribtuion that we wrote p(x, y | theta), then we'd
have a case for putting two things on the left.

It's just the way (Bayesian) statisticians write these functions.  And don't
worry, Andrew, we're not going to write normal(y; mu, sigma) as an alternative
for models intended for max likelihood estimation.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 31, 2015, at 11:20 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob!
>
> This sounds like a huge thing - is it worth investing this effort?

The biggest effort's going to be in rewriting all the doc.  And
the models, but we already want to do both of those things anyway,
so now's the time to change the language.  We've been discussing this
for a while and we've been holding off on updating models for this
reason.  It's terrible to be frozen waiting for a big change.

> Also, the deprecation period is hopefully very long,

The deprecation may be short --- as in introducing it in 2.10 and then dropping
it some time next year when we bring out Stan 3.  But so far, we don't know.
My worry is that people will keep using the old notation.

The bigger worry is that any book, etc., with a Stan model will be
out of date as soon as we do this.  My impression is that I'm the one
most concerned with breaking backward compatibility, but I may be wrong.

Stan 3's the time to change things if at all (though it doesn't necessarily
mean we have to break backward compatibility).

> i.e. Stan programs will look very different wrt to BUGS programs with this.

That's a feature, not a bug (see below).

> My comments:
>
> 1. Why introduce another logic with "<norm=true/false>"? Do you plan to introduce further options here, then it makes sense. If only for discriminating between normed/unnormed I would prefer a _norm naming convention thing.

Right now,

  y ~ foo(theta);

drops normalizing constants but

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y, theta));

keeps them.  We'd like to be able to control the behavior on
a case-by-case behavior.

The confusing bit's still going to be that our densities are
on the unconstrained scale with Jacobians, even if they get
the normalizing constants.

> 2. What is the rationale to introduce two new operators "<<" and ","?

The rationale was to make it clearer that everything in
Stan is just incrementing a log density.  So instead of having
both sampling statements and increment_log_prob statements, we
just have the log density accumulator.

The problem we have now is that people interpret the "~" as random
number generation or as graphical model building and sometimes just
copying BUGS and hoping things will work.  Instead, we want to emphasize
that a Stan program is just a regular imperative program defining
a log density.

- Bob

> Maybe I haven´t understood fully, but writing
>
> lp << density1 << density2;
>
> makes more sense to me.

The notation

  lp << a, b, c, d;

is from Eigen.  C++ output streams would be

  lp << a << b << c;

which I don't think anyone's going to like.

> In any case, I suggest to try out this new scheme on people who are more statisticians than programmers,

Andrew's the one who's been lobbying most strongly for it!

> i.e. I think someone having a programming background will absorb this easily, but I am not so sure about those people without a programming background.

Stan's a programming language, so I'm not so worried about people
who don't think they're doing programming or haven't done it before.

- Bob

On Saturday, January 2, 2016 at 9:25:28 AM UTC-5, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Vertical bar:
> - will there be any ambiguity with the or operator?

I've been trying to figure out how to express my objection and I think it's related to this.  There already is a well-established separator for function arguments in programming and for better or worse it's a comma (almost?) everywhere.  I don't think that programming syntax is the place to correct statistical thinking when it's going to cause syntax errors and mailing list traffic.

I'm trying to come up with another example where a programming language uses a syntactic choice to make a conceptual point that can't be inferred without consulting an outside source....  dplyr (well, magrittr) did this sort of thing in R by introducing a <- b %>% c as a way of stringing together arbitrary operations but a) that matches the way people (at least the "data science" people I know) think about data operations, it doesn't try to change it b) it builds on existing streaming concepts; and  c) it's still screwy because the final assignment is on the ultimate LHS.

In any multi-level setting you can't even think about the LHS of the bar as an observable so is the goal here to get people to think/admit that they're specifying a model in terms of conditional distributions?  Does forcing thinking in terms of conditional probabilities still make sense if specifying the model requires extra computations that increment the log probability through other functions?  Is there a specific user mistake we're trying to avoid?

I get that most of the developers are on board with this notation, I just don't get it given the costs (mostly in terms of mailing list traffic where the answer is going to be some polite version of RTFM/RTFAQ).

Krzysztof

There already is a well-established separator for function arguments in programming and for better or worse it's a comma (almost?) everywhere.  I don't think that programming syntax is the place to correct statistical thinking when it's going to cause syntax errors and mailing list traffic.
>
> I'm trying to come up with another example where a programming language uses a syntactic choice to make a conceptual point that can't be inferred without consulting an outside source....

I'm not sure what you mean by "inferred" here.  Pretty much
everything in a programming language syntax needs to be looked
up.

We could also allow "," in this context, but I think that'd be
even more confusing.

R uses %*% for matrix multiplication, and you certainly need
to look that up, but I don't think it's trying to make a conceptual
point (other than that matrix multiplication is a different function
and they'd already decided that plain old * acted elementwise).

C/C++/Java use | vs. || and & vs. && to differentiate bitwise
vs. logical disjunction and conjuncation.  But I think the reason
there is that they give different answers for integer inputs.

C++ uses a -> b to resolve a pointer, but a.b to resolve a reference.
All need to be looked up before using the language.

> In any multi-level setting you can't even think about the LHS of the bar as an observable

That's not the point;  if we wanted to do that, we'd use the semicolon :-)

It's that the | indicates conditioning --- hence its effect on normalization.

> so is the goal here to get people to think/admit that they're specifying a model in terms of conditional distributions?

No, just to make it easier to read models!

>  Does forcing thinking in terms of conditional probabilities still make sense if specifying the model requires extra computations that increment the log probability through other functions?  Is there a specific user mistake we're trying to avoid?

We certainly don't force anyone to think in terms of conditional densities.
You can write everything out via increment-log-prob if you want.

> I get that most of the developers are on board with this notation, I just don't get it given the costs (mostly in terms of mailing list traffic where the answer is going to be some polite version of RTFM/RTFAQ).

I'm guessing this isn't going to be a big deal on the mailing list.
We'll only get our answer if we introduce the bar!

- Bob

Luckily, our "or" operator is "||", so it won't be a problem.
We don't have the bitwise or-operator "|".  And all the parsing
is left-to-right, top-down, and greedy, so

  foo(a || b | c)

will get parsed as

  foo((a || b) | c)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new density notation
messages.body_plain:
I think everyone is OK with:

  * densities need some suffix

  * it should not be "_log"

  * log-scale should be explicitly indicated

I don't think there's a consensus on what the suffixes should
be, but Aki's right that we should look at the whole family.
I think his proposal makes a lot of sense:

   pdf  /  cdf /  ccdf /  dcdf
  lpdf  / lcdf / lccdf / ldcdf

I somehow think the "f" is redundant --- I assume we can at
least assume our users know what a function is --- but then it's in
common usage.

Is everyone OK with that?  And with using "pdf" for both density
and mass functions?  (Yes, they're all densities with the right
math, however the textbooks say "pmf").

What I don't think there's consensus on is

  * using a vertical bar, as in:

    normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma)

Also, I don't think there's consensus on the whole "<<" business,
as in:

  ld << ...;   // Michael
  << ...;      // Aki
  ld += ...;   // Krzysztof

Krzysztof thinks the vertical bar and << will confuse non-programmers.

And should that "ld" match "pdf" or vice-versa?

I think some people are thinking we might add other accumulators like
lprior or llikelihood (there's that pesky "l" for "log" again), or
maybe "lbase" and "ldelta".

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Aaaaaaah.  Do we need official minutes?  Almost all of these
issues were introduced in the last discussion of the proposed
changes.

> I don't think there's a consensus on what the suffixes should
> be, but Aki's right that we should look at the whole family.
> I think his proposal makes a lot of sense:
>
>   pdf  /  cdf /  ccdf /  dcdf
>  lpdf  / lcdf / lccdf / ldcdf
>
> I somehow think the "f" is redundant --- I assume we can at
> least assume our users know what a function is --- but then it's in
> common usage.
>
> Is everyone OK with that?  And with using "pdf" for both density
> and mass functions?  (Yes, they're all densities with the right
> math, however the textbooks say "pmf”).

The problem with differentiating between pdfs and pmfs is that
people will get confused about whether the posterior is a pdf or
a pmf.  It’s always a pdf for the models you can build in Stan,
but it’s not trivial to grok what goes where (pdfs over parameters,
hence prior or posterior, pdfs over data, pmfs over data).  Then
again, being more explicit may provide an opportunity for more
clear error messages, such as when a user tries to use a pmf
over parameters.

Things become even more complicated when we use CDFs,
because they are fundamentally different from densities.

If we want to be more explicit and we don’t mind the extra typing
then I’d say go with

pdf  /  cdf /  ccdf /  dcdf
lpdf  / lcdf / lccdf / ldcdf

with the understanding that not all may be implemented.

The f is technically redundant, but if we drop it then we’re
comparing pd and cd which are nonstandard and confusing
given the dual use of “d”.

> Krzysztof thinks the vertical bar and << will confuse non-programmers.

If anything “|” will confuse more programmers than users.  And
“<<“ is no less intuitive for non-programmers than “+=“.

> And should that "ld" match "pdf" or vice-versa?

If we go with a more explicit choice then yes, it should become lpdf.

On Sunday, January 3, 2016 at 2:18:39 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Also, I don't think there's consensus on the whole "<<" business,

>
>   ld << ...;   // Michael
>   << ...;      // Aki
>   ld += ...;   // Krzysztof

I'm fine with ld << ...;

If we want stats paper look, e.g.

ld << cauchy(tau | 0, 2.5),
        normal(beta | 0, 2),
        bernoulli_logit(y | x * (tau * beta));

then here << is better than +=, because += would imply summing distributions (not log densities). So the corresponding version with += would look like

ld += cauchy_lpdf(tau | 0, 2.5),
        normal_lpdf(beta | 0, 2),
        bernoulli_logit_lpdf(y | x * (tau * beta));

this latter form is more explicit and it migh be more natural if other than built-in distributions are used, e.g.

ld += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma) -log(sigma)

but maybe we could use << as

ld << normal(y | mu, sigma), 1/sigma

so that _lpdf's will be used if they are available and otherwise log of the expression is used. Yes, there is possibility of confusion by using both << and +=, but it would give possiblity for both stat paper look and more explicit log density construction.

Aki

No, no, no.  No automated processing, especially conditional processing.  That is ripe for confusion.  A stream operator is nice because it gives the notion of "adding" a new component to the target without specifying the representation.  Yes, it will always be log densities for us, but it's nice to abstract the concept to reinforce pedagogy.

When moving beyond standard distributions the user is on their own in ensuring validity.  Any processing on our part can give the user a false sense of security here which we definitely don't want.

I agree that we want the right-hand side to be any old expression.
So whatever is used for a density in place of A/B/C will just
be added to the log density.

+= is common, just not in R or BUGS or JAGS, so for
this particular audience, not so common.

I'm OK with not having a comma.  You can think of it
as streaming in a vector, which is what we do now with

  vector[N] x;
  ...
  increment_log_prob(x)

which is equivalent to

  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(x[n]);

So I guess another question is whether we allow vectors
on the right-hand-side of <<.

>> Krzysztof thinks the vertical bar and << will confuse non-programmers.
>
> I think I figured out from Michael's comments that the bar is adding a piece of information about the function not available anywhere else (except the manual).  I still don't understand if users are making a modeling mistake that this distinction helps to resolve but I'm ok with not knowing that.

No modeling mistake, just the convention p(y | theta)
for conditional densities as opposed to p(y, theta) for
joint densities.  And normal(y | mu, sigma) is the
conditional of y given mu and sigma in the sense that
for fixed sigma > 0 and any mu, it integrates to 1 over y.

- Bob

>
> then here << is better than +=, because += would imply summing distributions (not log densities). So the corresponding version with += would look like
>
> ld += cauchy_lpdf(tau | 0, 2.5),
>        normal_lpdf(beta | 0, 2),
>        bernoulli_logit_lpdf(y | x * (tau * beta));
>
> this latter form is more explicit and it migh be more natural if other than built-in distributions are used, e.g.
>

>
> but maybe we could use << as
>
> ld << normal(y | mu, sigma), 1/sigma
>
> so that _lpdf's will be used if they are available and otherwise log of the expression is used. Yes, there is possibility of confusion by using both << and +=, but it would give possiblity for both stat paper look and more explicit log density construction.

I don't want that much context sensitivity.  I really want
normal(y | mu, sigma) to be assignable, so that if
we allow

  ld << normal(y | mu, sigma)

then we'd also allow expressions like

  sum <- sum + normal(y[n] | mu, sigma);

and the normal would be on the log scale.  But everyone's
convinced me that's too confusing and we'll need a suffix
to sort out which function associated with the normal distribution
that we mean.

Also, we want to control the way the log density is coded
and taking logs would leave too much up to the compiler.

- Bob

messages.subject: log densities
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I agree with Bob that there’s a tension here.  In BDA, normal(a|b,c^2) has a clearly defined meaning.  In Stan, we’re changing things in two ways, and both are good:  we’re moving from variance to sd parameterization (thus, normal(a|b,c)), and we’re working with log densities.  In BDA notation:  lp(theta|y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y|theta).  So as long as we make it clear that normal(a|b,c) is lp, we’re good.  I agree with Bob that it would be good if normal(a|b,c) just represents this lp quantity.  This is the cleanest way to go.  And in this case I’d prefer not to have a _log suffix, as this would imply that not logging is the default.  To be clean, we should never allow a density or probability function in Stan to compute a non-logged density. This just means we need to be able to handle zero density values using -Inf on the log scale.  I assume we can do this?
A

> that we mean.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log densities
messages.body_plain:
Yes, we can use -inf on the log scale, but that
causes rejection and is always due to either a misspecified
model or arithmetic issues resulting in what Michael (and now
Stan) calls "divergent" transitions.

How do we make it clear that normal(y | mu, sigma) means
what everyone else writes as "log(normal(y | mu, sigma))"?
I was originally leaning toward having normal() be
a synonym (alias) for for normal_lpdf(), but now I'm
leaning toward it being too confusing if it's not packed
right into the name.  They might not know what "lpdf" means
at first glance, but at least it'll indicate that there's
something going on.

Took me a while to unpack lp as log p() and the rest as Bayes's rule:

> lp(theta|y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y|theta)

I don't see how that's relevant.

We don't have the non-log forms of the densities because they're
so unstable arithmetically.  We do have the non-log forms of the CDFs,
but I think that's a mistake in retrospect for the same reason.
The only problem is that we don't have the kind of numerical algorithm
expertise (or perhaps interest) to write stable log CDFs and log CCDFs
with derivatives.

- Bob

> On Jan 4, 2016, at 4:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

To be clean, we should never allow a density or probability function in Stan to compute a non-logged density. messages.body_plain:
I would argue that it’s a fine name.  We’re trying to specify
a model via a posterior, p(parameters | data), which means
defining inputs (data, parameters) and then the posterior
itself (model).  Other blocks are just convenient intermediates.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log densities
messages.body_plain:
Could we use Boost distribution functions?
They give error rates for CDFs, see, e.g.
http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_60_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/dist_ref/dists/nc_t_dist.html

Boost doesn't include log versions, not even for pdf, but I guess most of the time they exponentiate as late as possible, so the code could be reused.

As the mainstream is to have linear scale functions, I think we need to be explicit about log. If we are explicit about log, the having linear version of the function should not be much additional work? They would be useful, e.g., in mixture models and in generated quantities.

Aki

> Boost doesn't include log versions, not even for pdf, but I guess most of the time they exponentiate as late as possible, so the code could be reused.
>
> As the mainstream is to have linear scale functions, I think we need to be explicit about log. If we are explicit about log, the having linear version of the function should not be much additional work? They would be useful, e.g., in mixture models and in generated quantities.
>
> Aki

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "program" vs. "model" for Stan 3
messages.body_plain:
Is the idea also to have support in Stan 3 for someone using 'program'
instead of 'model' for that block (i.e., in the program code itself).

Thanks,

-a

On 01/04, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The name "model" for that block was a bad choice.
>
> The log density is actually implemented on the unconstrained
> params, and has terms that can be defined in any of the blocks.
> The log Jacobian for the transforms is added automatically and
> other terms are added in the model block, but subexpressions can
> come from all the other blocks.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jan 4, 2016, at 4:59 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Yes I’ve thought for awhile that it was unfortunate that we used the term “model” for the block of the Stan code that computes lp.  Since that block is the “model,” we use “program” to refer to the entire Stan program with all its blocks.
> >
> >> On Jan 4, 2016, at 10:25 AM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
> >>
> >> Just double checking about this:
> >>
> >> So when we (in Stan 2.x days) talked about 'parameters {real y;} model
> >> {y ~ normal(0,1);}' as "model code" (which typically was associated with
> >> a model name like `anon_model`) we should instead (in Stan 3) refer to
> >> this as "program code" associated with a "program name"? For example,
> >> the (Python) signature for the StanProgram constructor (née StanModel)
> >> should be `StanProgram(program_code, program_name)`. If so, is the goal
> >> eventually to have this reflected in the C++ API as well (`model_name`
> >> occurs in 13 files under the stan tree)?
> >>
> >> Best,
> >>
> >> Allen
> >>
> >>
> >> On 01/04, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >>> [moved to stan-dev]
> >>>
> >>> Absolutely.  I think the terminology we want to follow
> >>> is that a Stan program is a concrete implementation of a model.
> >>>
> >>> Now we have to be careful with reparameterizations, which
> >>> technically change the model if the model is defined as
> >>> the density on the unconstrained scale, but can be set up
> >>> in such a way as to maintain all the inferences we care about
> >>> from the original model.
> >>>
> >>> - Bob
> >>>
> >>>> On Jan 2, 2016, at 8:32 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
> >>>>
> >>>> Hi Bob,
> >>>>
> >>>> I really like the distinction between "model" and "program" that you

> >>>> Best,

> >>>> Allen

messages.subject: RStan Release Process
messages.body_plain:
We need to formalize the RStan release process, or at least fix
how dependencies work on CRAN.  I gave a tutorial today with
about 50 attendees that was fucked because most of them
(not surprisingly) waited until the last second to install RStan
from CRAN and all got bit by the RStan/StanHeaders clash.
Besides the embarrassment it took substantial amount of time
away from the tutorial.  We have to be able to do better.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RStan Release Process
messages.body_plain:
I understand the limitations of CRAN, but we need to find
some way around it.

For example, why were the dependencies updated so early?
Shouldn’t StanHeaders have been submitted first, and then
only when it had been built and deployed RStan submitted?

If there’s no way to ensure a consistent way to propagate
changes to the dependencies then we at least need a status
alert somewhere, whether it be on Jenkins or the mailing
list or Twitter where (a) these kinds of submit windows can
be announced and (b) queried at any time to make it easy
to identify that it’s a CRAN issue.

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, January 6, 2016 at 11:49:52 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I agree.  At least that way we’d know what was going on instead of getting
> weird compiler errors.

Refusing to install would be slightly better than installing but not working. But it means that it is impossible for me to do a patch fix of StanHeaders without also updating rstan, which could be a problem with the embargo on uploads within a month. In other words, if some function in Math was returning the wrong result, I could have done a StanHeaders 2.8.0-1 while leaving rstan 2.8.2 as is. So, if we have to utilize workarounds to get it to actually work during the major transition periods, I would rather maintain the ability to update them asynchronously when they don't break.

Ben

in any computational process with decent warning messages.

It's been an ongoing ugly transition since Python 3.0
was officially released way back in 2008 because of the
lack of backward compatibility.  The Python project has
been trying to get people off 2.x for over 7 years!  When
I worked on a project in 2010 or so, I couldn't use 3.x
because of client issues with it (it was natural language
processing).

>From the current Python 2 vs. Python 3 notes on python.org <http://python.org> (my highlighting):

     Guido van Rossum (the original creator of the Python language)
     decided to clean up Python 2.x properly, with less regard for
                                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
     backwards compatibility than is the case for new releases in
     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
     the 2.x range. The most drastic improvement is the better
     Unicode support (with all text strings being Unicode by default) as
     well as saner bytes/Unicode separation.

     However, the broader Python ecosystem has amassed a significant amount
     of quality software over the years. The downside of breaking backwards
     compatibility in 3.x is that some of that software (especially in-house
     software in companies) still doesn't work on 3.x yet.
                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Julia's now simultaneously working on versions 0.4
and 0.5, with no backward compatiblity and packages forking
based on version, with some people still stuck on 0.3 (though
I have no idea how many).   At Julia Con, the main devs spent a lot of
time discussing backward-compatibility breaking changes.  I'd
be way too timid to start developing in Julia now.  Julia has
this for 0.3 to 0.4 transitions:

  https://github.com/JuliaLang/Compat.jl

but I don't know if it works and is certainly got to be a major
hassle to implement.  There's a summary on that page's README about
how much has changed from 0.3 to 0.4.  But see this discussion on reddit:

  https://www.reddit.com/r/Julia/comments/2zme0y/timeframe_on_productionready_release_of_julia/

where 0.4 is described as the "break everything" release.  But then

  Regardless of the final scope of 0.4, 0.5 is going to have quite a
  few major changes in it that were holdovers that didn't make it into 0.4.

But lets just say their referring to 0.5 as "Arraypocalypse" had me worried.
(I'm neither Australian nor Alfred E. Neuman.):

  https://github.com/JuliaLang/julia/issues/13157

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log densities
messages.body_plain:
The way Boost is templated, we can autodiff the approximation
to function foo(x).  But precision bounds on foo(x) don't tell
us anything about precision bounds on the derivative foo'(x)
resulting from autodiffing the approximation to foo().

The right thing to do is develop a new approximate algorithm for
foo'(x).  But Boost hasn't done that.  Ditto for inverse CDFs.

For example, differentiating beta_cdf(y, alpha, beta) w.r.t. y
is easy, but it's much trickier w.r.t. alpha and beta.

- Bob

> On Jan 5, 2016, at 1:16 PM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, January 5, 2016 at 6:39:06 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> We are leaning heavily on Boost.  But they don't do derivatives.
>
> But you could copy the algorithms written in C++, and just add derivatives?
> Reading the code it seems that have thought about precision of the algorithms used and explain the choices in comments.
>
> Aki
>
>
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Jan 5, 2016, at 4:10 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>>>
>>> Could we use Boost distribution functions?
>>> They give error rates for CDFs, see, e.g.
>>> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_60_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/dist_ref/dists/nc_t_dist.html
>>>
>>> Boost doesn't include log versions, not even for pdf, but I guess most of the time they exponentiate as late as possible, so the code could be reused.
>>>
>>> As the mainstream is to have linear scale functions, I think we need to be explicit about log. If we are explicit about log, the having linear version of the function should not be much additional work? They would be useful, e.g., in mixture models and in generated quantities.
>>>
>>> Aki
>>>
>>> On Tuesday, January 5, 2016 at 9:40:31 AM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>>> We’re not getting good log CDF implementations anytime soon unless
>>>> we hire an army of mathematical programmers.
>>>>
>>>> On Jan 4, 2016, at 11:57 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> Yes, my current inclination is to have everything on the log scale, as that makes all explanations and notation simpler!  And, as you know, explanations and notation count for a lot!
>>>>>
>>>>>> On Jan 4, 2016, at 5:55 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Do you think we should get rid of the non-log forms altogether in
>>>>>> the language and make people apply exp() to the log-form if they
>>>>>> want it on the linear scale?
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Everyone agrees CDFs and CCDFs should have arithmetically stable log forms.
>>>>>> (And that we should have inverse CDFs for fun with reparameterizations.)
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Right now, our log forms are only as stable as the linear forms because
>>>>>> they just literally apply log(foo_cdf(...)) and log1m(foo_cdf(...)).
>>>>>>
>>>>>> We need someone to code the robust versions.
>>>>>>
>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Jan 4, 2016, at 5:33 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> I think it would be best for everything including cdfs to be in log forms but we can discuss.
>>>>>>> A
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> On Jan 4, 2016, at 5:32 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Yes, we can use -inf on the log scale, but that
>>>>>>>> causes rejection and is always due to either a misspecified
>>>>>>>> model or arithmetic issues resulting in what Michael (and now
>>>>>>>> Stan) calls "divergent" transitions.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> How do we make it clear that normal(y | mu, sigma) means
>>>>>>>> what everyone else writes as "log(normal(y | mu, sigma))"?
>>>>>>>> I was originally leaning toward having normal() be
>>>>>>>> a synonym (alias) for for normal_lpdf(), but now I'm
>>>>>>>> leaning toward it being too confusing if it's not packed
>>>>>>>> right into the name.  They might not know what "lpdf" means
>>>>>>>> at first glance, but at least it'll indicate that there's
>>>>>>>> something going on.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Took me a while to unpack lp as log p() and the rest as Bayes's rule:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> lp(theta|y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y|theta)
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> I don't see how that's relevant.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> We don't have the non-log forms of the densities because they're
>>>>>>>> so unstable arithmetically.  We do have the non-log forms of the CDFs,
>>>>>>>> but I think that's a mistake in retrospect for the same reason.
>>>>>>>> The only problem is that we don't have the kind of numerical algorithm
>>>>>>>> expertise (or perhaps interest) to write stable log CDFs and log CCDFs
>>>>>>>> with derivatives.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> On Jan 4, 2016, at 4:53 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> Yes, I agree with Bob that there’s a tension here.  In BDA, normal(a|b,c^2) has a clearly defined meaning.  In Stan, we’re changing things in two ways, and both are good:  we’re moving from variance to sd parameterization (thus, normal(a|b,c)), and we’re working with log densities.  In BDA notation:  lp(theta|y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y|theta).  So as long as we make it clear that normal(a|b,c) is lp, we’re good.  I agree with Bob that it would be good if normal(a|b,c) just represents this lp quantity.  This is the cleanest way to go.  And in this case I’d prefer not to have a _log suffix, as this would imply that not logging is the default.  To be clean, we should never allow a density or probability function in Stan to compute a non-logged density. This just means we need to be able to handle zero density values using -Inf on the log scale.  I assume we can do this?
>>>>>>>>> A
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> On Jan 4, 2016, at 2:27 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> I don't want that much context sensitivity.  I really want
>>>>>>>>>> normal(y | mu, sigma) to be assignable, so that if
>>>>>>>>>> we allow
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> ld << normal(y | mu, sigma)
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> then we'd also allow expressions like
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> sum <- sum + normal(y[n] | mu, sigma);
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> and the normal would be on the log scale.  But everyone's
>>>>>>>>>> convinced me that's too confusing and we'll need a suffix
>>>>>>>>>> to sort out which function associated with the normal distribution
>>>>>>>>>> that we mean.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Also, we want to control the way the log density is coded
>>>>>>>>>> and taking logs would leave too much up to the compiler.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] log densities
messages.body_plain:
We didn't really have a quorum for this discussion.

Andrew's opinion during the meeting was:

  a) always compute normalization terms for output of log-density;
     never compute normalization where not needed in the model block;
     continue to include normalization in generated quantities

  b) everything is on the log scale and there simply aren't
     non-log-scale functions, so they don't need to be marked

Both of these are contentious points.

Daniel suggested doing (a) without too much overhead by just recomputing
the model block once per iteration using double values.

If Andrew gets his way, that'd be:

  normal_pdf(y | mu, sigma) : log density

  normal_cdf(y ??? mu, sigma)  : log cdf

  normal_ccdf(y ??? mu, sigma) : log ccdf

  normal_inv_cdf(y ??? mu, sigma) : log inverse cdf

This would change the behavior of the existing functions normal_cdf()
in a non-backward-compatible way.

Then I believe Andrew wanted to allow "normal" as an abbreviation
for "normal_pdf".

- Bob

The issue is whether we even have non-log versions of pdf, cdf, and ccdf.

I'd strongly prefer not to have multiple ways to write basic functions.
If both normal(a | b, c) and normal_log(a | b, c) are in play, then users

the former is not on the log scale.  As Aki has pointed out, if we just
write normal(a | b, c), then everyone's going to assume it's *not* on the
log scale from looking at it.  He's right, and this is a big big step.

As to inverse CDFs, you're right that it doesn't make sense to have log
output.  But what about logit input?  Or do we have complementary inverse
cdfs to deal with the overflow to 1 problem on the 1 side of (0,1)?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Won't that depend on how we write the code?  I don't know anything
about this case, but I don't see any obstacle in principle to using
probabilities near 0 or 1 in inverse CDFs as long as the output doesn't
overflow or underflow.

But if we have something like gamma_inv_cdf(epsilon, a, b) and epsilon is
close to 0, then the output's going to be close to zero.  Or if we write
beta_inv_cdf(epsilon, a, b) and epsilon is close to 1, then the output is
close to 1 and it cries out for a a complementary inverse CDF on the log
scale for input and output.

Anyway, we can put off CDFs for the time being because we don't have any
implemented or any path to implement them until someone has some time
and energy for it.

- Bob

That works.  And if anyone wants to compute the normal pdf (for example, if they’re defining a mixture model), they’d just have to bite the bullet and do exp(normal(a | b, c)).
> Is that ok?

Sorry, I lost a bit of what you were suggesting. I think:
normal(a | b, c) should be in R: dnorm(a, b, c, log = TRUE)
normal_cdf(a | b, c) should be in R: pnorm(a, b, c, log=TRUE)

These things will result in a compiler error because they won't exist:
normal_log(a | b, c)
normal_lpdf(a | b, c)
normal_log_cdf(a | b, c)

Are we on the same page?

And yes, if they really, really want things on the normal scale (what's this called? exponentiated scale? probability scale? sorry... it's late and I can't think of the appropriate terminology), they will have to exponentiate.

So far, we've been carrying around two notations and it's just made it harder to think about. Of course, we're not doing this with other functions, just with the probability distributions. It's not like the sin() operator will return the log of the sin(), but I think it's ok since we're treating conditional distribution calls as first class citizens in the language.

Right now, my opinion is that all our distribution functions should be on the log scale. This includes:
- probability distribution / mass function
- cumulative distribution function
- inverse cumulative distribution function

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] notation for log densities
messages.body_plain:
Actually I was proposing something slightly different:

normal(a | b, c) should be in R: dnorm(a, b, c, log = TRUE)

normal_cdf(a | b, c) should be in R: pnorm(a, b, c, log=FALSE)
normal_log_cdf(a | b, c) should be in R: pnorm(a, b, c, log=TRUE)

But your plan could work too.  I’d like to avoid the _pdf or _lpdf suffix in any case because that would clutter the model.  To me, the #1 thing is getting the commonly-used distributions in a clean format, then we worry about things like cdfs being logical.

As I was saying at meeting on Tues, the main Bayes formula is p(theta | y) propto p(theta) p(y | theta).

But now I’d like to write it as lp(theta | y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y | theta).

In which case it’s clear that normal, poisson, binomial, etc., are just the lp’s.

As with our sd/variance notation, we’re making Stan inconsistent with BDA, and that’s too bad, but I think it’s worth it because of the transparency of the future Stan models.

That works.  And if anyone wants to compute the normal pdf (for example, if they’re defining a mixture model), they’d just have to bite the bullet and do exp(normal(a | b, c)).
> > Is that ok?
>
>

> normal_cdf(a | b, c) should be in R: pnorm(a, b, c, log=TRUE)

> normal_log(a | b, c)
> normal_lpdf(a | b, c)
> normal_log_cdf(a | b, c)
>
> Are we on the same page?
>
>
> And yes, if they really, really want things on the normal scale (what's this called? exponentiated scale? probability scale? sorry... it's late and I can't think of the appropriate terminology), they will have to exponentiate.
>
> So far, we've been carrying around two notations and it's just made it harder to think about. Of course, we're not doing this with other functions, just with the probability distributions. It's not like the sin() operator will return the log of the sin(), but I think it's ok since we're treating conditional distribution calls as first class citizens in the language.

> Right now, my opinion is that all our distribution functions should be on the log scale. This includes:
> - probability distribution / mass function

Not for inverse CDF, which can be a negative number, and even if the distribution is defined as positive, its log is not what any user would expect.

Ben

The decision regarding the cdfs must be made at the same time. We don't want to change the language twice.

I'm thinking about how to write a truncated model. I was really thinking about something like:

lp(mu, sigma | y, upper) = const + normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(upper | mu, sigma)

I think we should have expressions for:
cdf
1 - cdf
cdf - cdf

So... something like:
  lp << normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(upper |  mu, sigma);
  lp << normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_1mcdf(lower |  mu, sigma);
  lp << normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(lower, upper |  mu, sigma);

Or something similar? (please forgive me if I switched the truncation direction)

  normal(y | mu, sigma) T[, upper]
  normal(y | mu, sigma) T[lower, ]
  normal(y | mu, sigma) T[lower, upper]

> On Jan 6, 2016, at 11:30 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> OK, we can discuss again.  I see where you’re coming from.  I guess it’s fine if normal(a | b, c) is the log density, then we’d also have normal_log_cdf(a | b, c) and normal_cdf(a | b, c).  That works.  And if anyone wants to compute the normal pdf (for example, if they’re defining a mixture model), they’d just have to bite the bullet and do exp(normal(a | b, c)).
> Is that ok?
>

We don't want to encourage anyone to ever use exp(normal(a | b, c)).
If they want a mixture model, they should use log_sum_exp as we
outline in the manual.

> As I was saying at meeting on Tues, the main Bayes formula is p(theta | y) propto p(theta) p(y | theta).
>
> But now I’d like to write it as lp(theta | y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y | theta).

We really need a "propto" on the log scale.  I've been trying to figure
out how to say it for years without writing "const +", which is awkward
because it uses a five-letter word where every other variable is a Greek or
roman letter.

> So... something like:
>   lp << normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(upper |  mu, sigma);
>   lp << normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_1mcdf(lower |  mu, sigma);
>   lp << normal(y | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(lower, upper |  mu, sigma);

But we'll use "ccdf" instead of "1mcdf".  But now the relation
is on the log scale, so with no logs in sight, that's

  exp(foo_ccdf(y | theta)) = exp(1 - exp(foo_cdf(y | theta)))

Normally it's just

  CCDF(...) = 1 - CDF(...)

> I think we also want to keep the T[] notation, but I could be convinced otherwise:
>   normal(y | mu, sigma) T[, upper]
>   normal(y | mu, sigma) T[lower, ]
>   normal(y | mu, sigma) T[lower, upper]

Absolutely.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] notation for log densities
messages.body_plain:
I am strongly with Bob and Dan.  Shortcuts for "commonly-used distributions" is another way of saying "inconsistent behavior based on contexts that can change in time".  Especially when those contexts are based on Andrew's rapidly evolving perspectives!  We want the language to be explicit as possible so it will be robust to our changing understanding and best practices.

On Jan 7, 2016, at 5:55 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Actually I was proposing something slightly different:
>
> normal(a | b, c) should be in R: dnorm(a, b, c, log = TRUE)
> normal_cdf(a | b, c) should be in R: pnorm(a, b, c, log=FALSE)
> normal_log_cdf(a | b, c) should be in R: pnorm(a, b, c, log=TRUE)
>
> But your plan could work too.  I’d like to avoid the _pdf or _lpdf suffix in any case because that would clutter the model.  To me, the #1 thing is getting the commonly-used distributions in a clean format, then we worry about things like cdfs being logical.
>
> As I was saying at meeting on Tues, the main Bayes formula is p(theta | y) propto p(theta) p(y | theta).
>
> But now I’d like to write it as lp(theta | y) = const + lp(theta) + lp(y | theta).
>
> In which case it’s clear that normal, poisson, binomial, etc., are just the lp’s.
>
> As with our sd/variance notation, we’re making Stan inconsistent with BDA, and that’s too bad, but I think it’s worth it because of the transparency of the future Stan models.
>

messages.subject: silly integral question
messages.body_plain:
I'm writing up a doc and have confused myself about computing
posterior predictive densities on the log scale.

I know for new data y', observed data y, and parameters theta that
the posterior predictive density is defined by

 p(y' | y) = INTEGRAL_Theta p(y' | theta) p(theta | y) d.theta.

But I (think I) want the log posterior density,

 log p(y' | y) = log INTEGRAL_Theta p(y' | theta) p(theta | y) d.theta.

But instead, what I wind up with if I define

  log_p <- log p(y' | theta)

in a Stan program will be this average:

  1/M SUM_{m in 1:M} log p(y' | theta[m])

where theta[m] is the m-th posterior draw for theta.  So
that corresponds to this integral:

 INTEGRAL_Theta (log p(y' | theta)) p(theta | y) d.theta.

which can't be the same given that log doesn't even distribute
through addition.

So I'm OK with the whole posterior of log p(y' | y), but the posterior
mean of that isn't the mean of the posterior of p(y' | y).

So how do I actually compute the posterior log density?  Is
it OK to just work with the expectation of the posterior log
density rather than the log of the expectation of the posterior density?

The immediate application is that I want to compare models based
on the log density on a held-out data set.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] silly integral question
messages.body_plain:
You can bound the log expectation by the expectation of the log using Jensen’s inequality,
but the bound may not be all that tight.  Interestingly enough, this discrepancy is a large
motivation behind WAIC — see http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf,
especially section 3.4, for how WAIC uses the expectation of the log to estimate the log
of the expectation.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] silly integral question
messages.body_plain:
To directly answer the question, you would have to exponentiate log posterior densities to weight the likelihood terms p(y’ | theta) with p(theta | y), then take the mean, and then take the log. This comes up a lot, e.g., I am/Andrew is doing this when calculating importance weights during GMO. To do log(sum(exp))s in a numerically reasonable manner, you should take the max of the logs, subtract by that max, and then do log(sum(exp))) on that difference.

Dustin

that it expresses model in the natural domain, but works in the log
domain, so * -> + and + -> log_sum_exp implicitly.

messages.subject: feedback on hierarchical model tutorial
messages.body_plain:
Before releasing to our users, I'd like to get some feedback
on a knitr doc I wrote as an intro to hierarchical modeling
for repeated binary trials.  It lives here:

  stan-dev/example-models/knitr/efron-morris/pool-no-pool.Rmd

As usual, I had a hard time judging what to explain and what
to take for granted.  I tried to focus on Stan.  Any tips on
making the RStan better would be appreciated.  Andrew, now's the
time to jump in on ggplot2 defaults!  Or I can ask you in person
and we can create a theme you can live with.

I'm happy to send the 2.8MB HTML file it produced (encapsulated)
if you'd rather not run it yourself.  (If you do want to run it,
you only need:

  > rmarkdown::render("pool-no-pool.Rmd")

to get the basic HTML.  I couldn't get it to keep the figures
separate, even trying what Ben suggested (I'm probably doing it
wrong).

Here's the abstract:

This note illustrates the effects on posterior inference of pooling
data (aka sharing strength) across items for repeated binary trial
data.  It provides Stan models and R code to fit and check predictive
models for three situations: (a) complete pooling, which assumes each
item is the same, (b) no pooling, which assumes the items are
unrelated, and (c) partial pooling, where the similarity among the
items is estimated.  We consider two hierarchical models to estimate
the partial pooling, one with a beta prior on chance of success and
another with a normal prior on the log odds of success.  The note
explains with working examples how to (i) fit models in RStan and plot
the results in R ussing ggplot2, (ii) estimate event probabilities,
(iii) evaluate posterior predictive densities to compare model
predictions, (iv) rank items by chance of success, (v) perform
multiple comparisons in several settings, (vi) replicate new data for
posterior p-values, and (vii) perform graphical posterior predictive
checks.

- Bob

messages.subject: updated log-density discussion
messages.body_plain:
I tried to include all the relevant discussion from the lists
and include pros and cons as raised:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments

Argument by argument, I'm personally leaning toward:

  * explicit suffixes for all probability-related functions

  * default to normalized densities

  * not getting clever with vertical bar

  * going with just ld for the accumulator

  * using += and switching assignment to = elsewhere

  * Getting Daniel to write a translator because these models
    are going to look way different

All in, the caterpillar we now write as

  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

transforms into the beautiful butterfly

   ld += normal_lpdf<norm=false>(y, mu, sigma);

Hang on a second.  I liked all those decisions until they
piled up into that trainwreck of a statement.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] updated log-density discussion
messages.body_plain:
I think that a lot of issues that are non-aesthetic (eg |, << vs +=)
revolve around choosing sensible defaults, or in other words, deciding
which use occurs frequently enough to warrant a shorter form.

Having read through the document in the wiki with this in mind, I
realized why I like the current syntax:

y ~ some_distribution(some_parameters);

is the kind of expression I need to write most often. I am not sure that
the language needs be super-explicit about emphasizing that we are in
fact incrementing a log density, in every single line.

I could also live with

some_distribution(y | some_parameters);

with the understanding that for statements that are not assignments or
shorthand for assignments (eg var+=), ld+= is assumed without making it
explicit.

Regarding <> keyword arguments: I am under the impression that blocks of
normalized statements tend to occur frequently in the same
block/expression. So one could introduce a prefix like

normalized [expression];

eg

normalized cauchy_lpdf(y | mu, tau);

or

normalized {
  ...a block of multiple such statements...
}

Similarly for vectorized, eg

log_lik <- normalized vector normal(y | mu, tau);

instead of

log_lik <- normal_lpdf<norm=true,vector=true>(y | mu, tau);

But I don't know how much this would complicate the parser.

Anyway, I think it would be instructive to have an example page of 2-5
programs that demonstrate the shortcomings of current syntax, and then
rewrite them with proposed syntaxes (rewriting done by those who make a
proposal for a syntax).

Best,

Tamas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] feedback on hierarchical model tutorial
messages.body_plain:
Section: Repeated Binary Trials

I would reference n \in N in the opening sentence, otherwise the n subscripts don’t make sense until the next few sentences have been read.

“any ML conference proceedings” or “all ML conference proceedings”?  :-p

Emphasize that you are using the remaining data to determine _predictive performance_.

Put “The data separates the outcome from the initial 45 at-bats from the rest of the season.” after the display of the data.  Perhaps something like “The data are separated into the first 45 at bats of the season and the remaining at bats; we will use the first 45 at bats to build our model and then the remaining at bats to test the predictive performance of our model.”

Section: Pooling

There’s an awkward line break after the first two sentences.

You haven’t defined a population distribution yet so the the discussion of variances has no context here.  If you wanted to include this note here, I would introduce another sentence like “Partial pooling is typically accomplished with a hierarchical or population model, where the individuals assumed to have been are drawn from a population normally distributed with mean mu and variance sigma2.  When the population variance is infinite partial pooling is equivalent to no pooling, while zero population variance is equivalent to complete pooling”.  Or just leave this discussion to the partial pooling section (although you don’t use a normal hierarchical model there, so the relevant of this point is questionable).

Section: Model 1: Complete Pooling

Do you want () or [] here? Typically 0 and 1 are considered valid values, in which case you want [0, 1].

“The consequences for leaving the constraint off is that the program may fail during random initialization or during an iteration because it will try values…” What is “it”?  Maybe something like “…because Stan will consider mathematically invalid values outside of (0, 1)”.

The proportion sign hasn’t been used yet, why is it being described here?

“The model can be fit as follows, reading…” -> “The model can be fit as follows: <fit input>”.  Note that the data are read out of the R environment by name…”

Section: Model 3: Partial Pooling (Chance of Success)

I recommend running with the default step size and adapt_delta and discuss the errors that show up.  Mention how the errors indicate that Stan isn’t fitting well and we can try to tweak the step size and adapt_delta to improve the fit.  It helps, but the mixing is still bad so we need a better solution (which then motivates the next section).

The Beta distribution isn’t a location-scale distribution so it is not immediately amenable to the centering/non-centering discussion.  But it can be manipulated into a location-scale family by unconstraining its parameters, in which case you center/non-center the unconstrained parameters.  Essentially you’ll end up with something like the model in the next section anyways.

Section: Model 4: Partial Pooling (Log Odds)

Yup, the distribution for mu and sigma will still look like a weak funnel (when the random effect variation is large, there is a weak non-identifiability between the mean and the average of the random effects).  What you want to be looking at is the distribution of the random effects, alpha, verses sigma.  That’s what causes all of the problems in the fit.

Section: Observed vs. Estimated Chance of Success

It would be great if more of the plot could be labeled to avoid having to describe everything in the text.

Section: Posterior Predictive Distribution

You never discuss what you can do with the predictive distribution, let alone why they provide a ranking that might approximate relative performance.  This leaves a big gap when you move on to the explicit calculations.

Section: Posterior p-Values

I highly recommend a comment here about how posterior predictive p-values can’t really be calibrated (no power calculations can be done because there is no alternative hypothesis).  This means that we can’t formally distinguish between a bad fit or unlikely data, and we have to be careful in how we interpret these values.  Ultimately what we do in practice is assume that for small enough p-values there has to be some alternative model that fits better, and if we see such small p-values we start looking for that alternate model by expanding our null model.

messages.subject: Stan 3 density notation: final stages
messages.body_plain:
I updated with respect to the Stan meeting discussion on Tuesday:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments

I think we're nearing agreement.  To summarize, the unnormalized
form is:

  target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);

and the normalized form is

  target += normal_lpdf<norm>(y | mu, sigma);

We add = for assignment and deprecate <- and support += generally, but
only allow target to be used on LHS with +=.

We change suffix _lp to _target and _log to _lpdf in user-defined functions.

We do not allow vectorization control (at least for now).

We do not add a special link=logit, etc. form of control.

All existing functionality still supported, but deprecated.  If we get
it in before Stan 3, we could just pull it out from under people in
Stan 3, or we could wait a year.  The downside is all the material written
using our existing notation;  the risk is that people will keep using
the existing notation, even if we deprecate it.

There are still a couple issues to resolve:

* vertical bar with lcdfs, lccdfs, and ldiff_cdfs?

* allow access to target as a value?

* allow vectors on RHS of += the way we do with increment_log_prob()?

Anyway, none of this will be at all challenging to build, though there's
going to have be a ton of tests around it to make sure it all works
and the deprecation warnings are right.

- Bob

>   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments
>
> I think we're nearing agreement.  To summarize, the unnormalized
> form is:
>
>   target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);
>
> and the normalized form is
>
>   target += normal_lpdf<norm>(y | mu, sigma);
>
> We add = for assignment and deprecate <- and support += generally, but
> only allow target to be used on LHS with +=.
>
> We change suffix _lp to _target and _log to _lpdf in user-defined functions.
>
> We do not allow vectorization control (at least for now).
>
> We do not add a special link=logit, etc. form of control.

After reading the summary this makes sense to me.

> All existing functionality still supported, but deprecated.  If we get
> it in before Stan 3, we could just pull it out from under people in
> Stan 3, or we could wait a year.  The downside is all the material written
> using our existing notation;  the risk is that people will keep using
> the existing notation, even if we deprecate it.
>
> There are still a couple issues to resolve:
>
> * vertical bar with lcdfs, lccdfs, and ldiff_cdfs?

Yes

> * allow access to target as a value?

Yes for print statements, no for anything else? The whole benefit of only allowing += is that
it's something you build up.

> * allow vectors on RHS of += the way we do with increment_log_prob()?

Seems confusing to me, I'd prefer no unless it would be a performance consideration for some reason?

> Anyway, none of this will be at all challenging to build, though there's
> going to have be a ton of tests around it to make sure it all works
> and the deprecation warnings are right.

> - Bob

On Friday, January 22, 2016 at 1:06:32 PM UTC-5, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> I'm curious to see what users' reactions will be when we change assignment from "<-" to "=" given that the majority of users seem to use the RStan interface and are used to "<-". Personally, I'm fine with making that change, as it brings Stan more in line with the overwhelming majority of programming languages, but I do think there is something nice about using "<-" for assignment, as "=" already has other uses unrelated to assignment.

If we do += for incrementing target, then it makes sense to use = for assignment. And it would be pretty easy for the parser to catch a <- and suggest changing it to =. And it is pretty easy for people to do a find-and-replace in their existing Stan programs. But it is a change that affects almost every line without providing a whole lot of benefit. Perhaps if there were more people in favor of the @ notation, we could keep <- for assignment.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] feedback on hierarchical model tutorial
messages.body_plain:
Bob, this is awesome. I finally had a chance to read through most of it.
I think the others have made good recommendations already, but I do have one
suggestion about the R code, which is that the with() function is very useful.
There are several places where it can make your code simpler:

1) You have:

df <- data.frame(FirstName = df$FirstName,
                 LastName = df$LastName,
                 Hits = df$Hits,
                 At.Bats = df$At.Bats,
                 RemainingAt.Bats = df$RemainingAt.Bats,
                 RemainingHits = df$SeasonHits - df$Hits)

but you can do the same thing like this:

df <- with(df, data.frame(FirstName, LastName,
                          Hits, At.Bats,
                          RemainingAt.Bats,
                          RemainingHits = SeasonHits - Hits))

which avoids the df$ on every line and the repetition of variable names (which are both pet peeves of mine, but maybe that's just me).

2) The same thing goes for working with the lists that rstan::extract returns. For
example, this

phi_sim <- ss_hier$phi;
kappa_sim <- ss_hier$kappa;
df_bda3_fig_5_3 <- data.frame(x = log(phi_sim / (1 - phi_sim)),
                              y = log(kappa_sim));

can be done in one line without the intermediate steps of creating phi_sim and
kappa_sim:

df_bda3_fig_5_3 <- with(ss_hier, data.frame(x = log(phi / (1 - phi)),
                                            y = log(kappa)))

3) You can do the same thing later in the file when working with the next model:

mu_sim <- ss_hier_logit$mu;
sigma_sim <- ss_hier_logit$sigma;
df_bda3_fig_5_3_logit <- data.frame(x = mu_sim,
                                    y = log(sigma_sim));

can all be replaced with the one line

df_bda3_fig_5_3_logit <- with(ss_hier_logit, data.frame(x = mu_sim,
                                    y = log(sigma_sim)))

Again, this really is a fantastic tutorial. And of course feel free to ignore my R code preferences. The way you have it now definitely works just fine.

Old habits die hard.  I don't even like ending lines
of R without a semicolon!

Only Python users (and makefile experts) are used to whitespace (tab)
indent, and even with nicely formatting text editors like emacs, it
can lead to errors.

The nice part about paren balancing is that editors highlight
the matching parens and do the indentation so you get
something like a checksum.  That's why I feel safe using no-paren
indents in our C++ code.

The downside of bracketsq is a bit of redundancy and wasted
vertical space for the close brackets.  And all in, I think
well-formatted Python is about the easiest code to read out
there.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There's been a lot of discussion. Here's where I stand:

Proposed suffixes:
- I'd prefer if the pdfs on the log scale were left without a suffix, but I think I'm the only one. I was thinking about treating lpdfs / lpmfs as first class objects that are always on the log scale. Yes, it doesn't run parallel with cdfs, but I was thinking about the most common use case and how Stan programs look. I'm assuming this idea won't be supported by anyone else and this will be the last I bring it up, unless someone else supports it.
- log pdf / pmf: I prefer _lp, but would be ok with _lpdf. Although I understand Michael's point about forcing the user to think about pdf vs pmf, I think it's going to cause confusion and slow down the process.

Vertical bar notation:
- yes. I don't know what to do with user-defined multivariate distributions, but we can figure that out later.

Normalization control:
- I prefer having "<norm>" and "". It saves space. I see the point about not being the best decision for adding other control, but it's either normalized or not.
- default: unnormalized. For speed.

Increment log density statement:
- one more vote for "target +="
- one downvote for @. Looks too much like an attribute to me.
- I want something on the left size. target seems right. Second choice: model.

Link functions:
- I'm ok with the proposed which is the same as what we have now.
- If we went with <>, would it be too confusing to drop the "link=" so we could do something like: poisson<log>... nm, I don't think this.

Misc:
- +1 for switching assignment from <- to =.
- +1 for += everywhere

This is the biggest drawback to "_pdf" --- I don't
like having to distinguish.  Especially since the two
options don't even partition the probability functions.
What we're really defnining as a model with a Stan
program is often the joint density of a combination of
discrete and continuous variables.

normalization and leaving it blank will leave in the template

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan 3 density notation: final stages
messages.body_plain:
> What we're really defnining as a model with a Stan
> program is often the joint density of a combination of
> discrete and continuous variables.

No no no no no no no.  I know Andrew likes thinking about
models this way due to the prior/likelihood ambiguities in
hierarchical models, but that’s not what we do in Stan.

Stan defines a conditional probability density function,
p(alpha | beta) where alpha are defined in the parameters
block (or functions there of) and beta are defined in data,
transformed data, or sometimes as local constants.  The
importance of this distinction, besides where the variables
are defined, is that alpha must be continuous while beta
can be continuous or discrete.

Sloppy equivalences like

p(alpha | beta) \propto p(alpha, beta)

make sense only when we keep this type distinction in
mind and can actually drop the intermediate constant.
If we were just defining a joint distribution then we could
write

p(alpha, beta) = p(alpha | beta) p(beta) \propto p(beta | alpha)
p(alpha, beta) = p(beta | alpha) p(alpha) \propto p(alpha | beta)

hence p(beta | alpha) and p(alpha | beta) would be
equivalent!  But Stan can define the only the latter
when any of the beta are discrete.

To be more formal, what we are defining is a disintegration of
the joint distribution p(alpha, beta) which requires more
information than the joint distribution itself.

Yes, it's the posterior distribution being targeted by MCMC but if

normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);

evaluates to some number like 0.12345 it is not as if

target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);

means something like "increase the posterior distribution by 0.12345". It means "increase the value of the log of the numerator in Bayes' theorem by 0.12345".

When maximizing, it is reasonably clear that the goal is to choose the values of the parameters to make the objective function as large as possible. I think "target" would be perceived by users as implying "I am adding 0.12345 to something in order to make it closer to its target".

Ben

Right --- there's an asymmetry between the data x and
parameters theta to put it back in Andrew's notation.
And what we care about is that the model returns
something that's proportional to

  target = log p(theta | x) + Z(x)

where we don't care about Z(x) [assuming the unconstraining
transforms and Jacobians].

All I'm saying is that if you code the model as usually
written and include the normalization terms, what you
get for lp__ (target) is log p(theta, x), not
log p(theta | x).

But what's cool about Stan is that you don't have to
code the model that way.  As long as whatever you code
is proportional to p(theta | x), you're good to go.

- Bob

>>> form is:

>>>
>>> target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);

>>> and the normalized form is
>>>
>>> target += normal_lpdf<norm>(y | mu, sigma);

>>> We add = for assignment and deprecate <- and support += generally, but

>>> We change suffix _lp to _target and _log to _lpdf in user-defined functions.

>>> We do not allow vectorization control (at least for now).
>>>
>>> We do not add a special link=logit, etc. form of control.
>>>
>>> All existing functionality still supported, but deprecated.  If we get
>>> it in before Stan 3, we could just pull it out from under people in
>>> Stan 3, or we could wait a year.  The downside is all the material written
>>> using our existing notation;  the risk is that people will keep using
>>> the existing notation, even if we deprecate it.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan 3 density notation: final stages
messages.body_plain:
It'll work just like any other program, like

  double f(double x, sigma) {
    double target = 0;
    target += -(x * x) / (sigma * sigma * 2);
    target -= log(sigma);
    return target;
  }

A variable is part of the function definition.  Given
an execution context and state of execution (for
instance, called with x = -1.2, sigma = 0.5,
done executing first two statements), it will have
a value.  So in a progamming language context, you
usually think of a variable as a mapping from
execution contexts (often modeled as some kind of
continuation) and a value.  The value will have a type
determined by the variable's type.

The big difference is that the target value in Stan
will underlying be an accumulator collecting a sequence
of values (usually autodiff variables) and will itself
have to be evaluated to get a result (the evaluation is
just summing, but we collect them up for efficiency to
reduce the size of the resulting expression graph).  Another
difference is that it's implicitly declared and initialized
(optionally) to the Jacobian of the constraining transform.

- Bob

> On Jan 22, 2016, at 5:52 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Friday, January 22, 2016 at 5:27:20 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Well “target distribution” is standard MCMC terminology and
> we can emphasize that in the doc.  Besides, we never actually
> add a number of the LHS — we’re always aggregating a function.
>
> I guess that is what I anticipate users finding confusing. The way the += syntax is used in non-Stan examples all over the internet suggests numbers rather than defining a function piece by piece that is within a constant of the log density of the posterior distribution being targeted by MCMC.
>
> Ben

>> “target distribution” is the MCMC equivalent of “objective function” in optimization.
>> In Bayesian inference the target distribution is the posterior, although Stan is
>> technically more general than that.  I’m not sure what you mean by the posterior
>> not being the thing that is being incremented — at any point if we stopped then
>> the current state of the LHS would be the target distribution.
>>

>>
>> normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);
>>
>> evaluates to some number like 0.12345 it is not as if
>>
>> target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);
>>
>> means something like "increase the posterior distribution by 0.12345". It means "increase the value of the log of the numerator in Bayes' theorem by 0.12345".

>> When maximizing, it is reasonably clear that the goal is to choose the values of the parameters to make the objective function as large as possible. I think "target" would be perceived by users as implying "I am adding 0.12345 to something in order to make it closer to its target".

Yes I think _lp should appended, so normal_lp() and normal_cdf_lp(). Levels of detail:

_lpdf / _lpmf / _lcdf
_lpdf / _lcdf
_log / _cdf_log (including _log_log)
_lp / _cdf_lp
(nothing) / _cdf

Most of us are okay with dropping the distinction between _lpdf and _lpmf due to its added confusion for users. I don’t think _log makes sense, one reason being the requirement of _log_log, and more generally that it’s doesn’t convey anything regarding density (“lognormal_log” is also strange). I think I’m okay with _lp because we’ve already been using log prob for so many things both code wise and user-wise, and so I/stan users have already internalized it. _log_pdf/log_cdf would be too verbose but any jumble that requires enunciating at least 4 characters seems a bit much both for typing and internalizing.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan 3 density notation: final stages
messages.body_plain:
I originally derived "lp__" from "log pdf" and "log pmf"
because Andrew calls pdfs and pmfs "probability functions"
in BDA and "lp__" was the internal accumulator for the log
probability function.   In retrospect, I regret that decision
because it's too easy to take it to mean "log probability", and
it's a density, not a probability.

The reason I don't like the unmarked case "normal(y | mu, sigma)"
for the log density is that I want the expression to just be a function,
and the function normal( | , ) is pretty much universally understood
in papers and textbooks to mean the linear scale.

I don't mind "lognormal_log", but "poisson_log_log" is pushing
things.  I also don't like neg_binomial_2, becuase like the link=log,
it's just another parameterization (though I don't think it's
considered a link function when you switch normal or gamma or negative
binomial parameterizations).

- Bob

P.S.  Why is "pdf" lower-cased?  It's not pronounced like
      a word, so even Andrew wouldn't lower-case it on
      first principles.  Maybe the early probability theory
      authors thought "PDF" everywhere looked tacky :-)

- Bob

labeled the Stan program itself can put errors into context.  You can’t have
pmfs with parameters left of the bar, or CDFs incremented into the target,

running into trouble.  All of this needs to be supported in the doc, but it
leads to a much cleaner user experience, especially for new users (it’s
always better to have a giant pile of material to read than not know what
your problem is).

Again, I’m not arguing for what is easier for _me_ to read/use, but rather
new users.
